title: Guard my tongue (Berakhot 17a)
hookLine: the closing prayer: my God, guard my tongue from evil
carry: let my soul be like dust

lines: COUNT WHAT GETS SAID ABOUT PEOPLE.
cards: A small experiment for the end of the day: count the things said about people who weren't in the room. The coworker's annoying habit. The friend's bad decision.
The relative everyone sighs about. The tally can climb fast. Now look at where the Amidah puts its last request.

The person praying has stood for several minutes, feet together, asking for wisdom, healing and peace. And as they get ready to step back into the day, the closing prayer worries first about one thing: the mouth.

teach.b: The Talmud, in Berakhot 16b and 17a, records the private prayers different rabbis said after they finished the Amidah. One of them, from Mar the son of Ravina, is the one printed in the prayer book today.
It begins: Elohai, netzor leshoni mera.
My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit. It's built on a psalm.
In the old Jewish translation: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile."

teach.h: OPEN MY LIPS, THEN GUARD THEM.
teach.b: Then: to those who curse me, let my soul be silent; let my soul be like dust to everyone. Open my heart to Your Torah. Notice the grammar has changed.
The Amidah's requests speak as we: heal us, forgive us, bring us back. This prayer says my.
My tongue. My soul. It began as one rabbi's personal prayer, and it still sounds like one.
It ends with another psalm: "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before Thee, O LORD, my Rock, and my Redeemer."
Then the three steps back, a bow to the left, the right and the center, and oseh shalom: may the one who makes peace on high make peace for us. Remember drew near, and sefatai tiftach?
The Amidah opened by asking God to open the mouth. It closes by asking God to guard it.

how: After the final blessing of the Amidah, Jews say Elohai netzor quietly, then Psalm 19:15, then take three steps back, bow left, right and center while saying oseh shalom, and stand a moment before stepping forward again.

o: a prayer to guard the home from harm
my God, guard: the prayer for a careful tongue
a vow of total silence for a whole day

games.q: inside the closing prayer — tap the pairs.
p: said with the three steps back

s: Elohai netzor speaks as we, like the Amidah's requests
it speaks as I: my tongue, my soul. it began as one rabbi's prayer.
the Talmud records several rabbis' personal prayers after the Amidah
Berakhot 16b–17a; Mar son of Ravina's became the common one.
the Amidah opens and closes with the mouth
open my lips at the start, guard my tongue at the end.

games.q: you've finished the Amidah's last blessing. someone at the door is gossiping about a neighbor. what does the closing prayer ask for first?
games.why: My God, guard my tongue from evil, and my lips from speaking deceit: the first thing asked on the way back into the day.

practice: Pick the next hour of your day that will have people in it, a meeting, a family dinner, a group chat, and decide now: for that hour, nothing unkind about someone who isn't there, no eye-rolls, no small digs.
Picture the moment the temptation will come, and the quiet you'll put in its place. If you pray, you can say the first line: my God, guard my tongue from evil.

wordCard.voice: Elohai Netzor. My God, guard. The personal prayer after the Amidah, asking to guard the tongue from evil.

orig.note: Hebrew: my God, guard. the opening words of the prayer after the Amidah.

carryVoice: Your line: let my soul be like dust. A week that prayed against harm, right beside the righteous, for Jerusalem, in your own words, with thanks, for peace, and now for a guarded tongue: the whole Amidah, walked. Day five hundred ninety-five.
